label: Stop 3: The Irish bar on Clark

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Okay, it's evening, and I've eaten a steak.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Where are we?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: You walked about six minutes northwest from Steak 48, along Ontario Street and Clark Street, to the corner of Clark and Erie.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: This is the Kerryman, an Irish bar.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Authentic Irish saloon, said the itinerary.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Careful there. The owners, two brothers from County Kerry, describe it more as a modern Irish cocktail lounge than an old pub.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It has a main bar, a mezzanine, and a second room that gets DJs on Friday and Saturday nights.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So not a cozy fireside.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Not exactly. But the building has a past.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In the 1920s this was a bar called McGovern's, and it was reportedly a hangout for Chicago's Prohibition-era gangsters.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In the late 1970s it reopened as a punk bar, and one source calls it the original Chicago punk bar.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: A punk bar, in a place with a steak house on the corner.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: River North was different then.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The name Kerryman, by the way, is said to come from Saint Brendan the Navigator, the Kerry saint who may have sailed the Atlantic.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Said to?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Even the source says it may be legend.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Same with Brendan's voyage. It's a medieval story, not documented history.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: I'm good with that. A saint, a punk bar, and a gangster rumor.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Tell me about the other option.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Well, there is one. If you'd rather see a Chicago Christmas tavern, you can take a cab about six minutes north to Butch McGuire's, at 20 West Division Street, in the Gold Coast.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And that's holiday decorated?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Very. Robert "Butch" McGuire opened it in 1961.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He borrowed five hundred and sixty dollars from his mother to buy a former speakeasy.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Five hundred and sixty dollars.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: For a bar.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It was a different century. He became known as the unofficial Mayor of Division Street.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He wanted a place where unescorted women were welcome, which was unusual then, and the bar claims it has led to more than six thousand five hundred marriages.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Claims. You said claims.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Because it's the bar's own count, not an independent one.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The Christmas decorations are the real draw, with about forty thousand lights.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: They go up in October and stay until mid-January, so in December you'll see them at their best.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So Kerryman is the stroll, and Butch is the cab.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Exactly. Either is fine.
